abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: With the ongoing trend toward miniaturization and high-density integration in electronic packaging, System-in-Package (SiP) has become a key research focus for large-scale AI model integration. This study investigates SiP packaging, focusing on warpage-induced stress during reflow soldering through detailed simulations. Unlike previous FEM approaches, this study integrates both viscoelastic dielectric modeling and trace mapping for realistic SiP reflow simulation, including actual copper trace layouts, viscoelasticity, and creep behavior, to develop an effective simulation model. Warpage and stress under complex conditions—such as varying dielectric layers, core substrate materials, and solder ball compositions—are thoroughly examined. The results indicate that simulations considering trace layouts and initial warpage offer significantly more accurate predictions than traditional models. For core substrate materials, the elastic modulus alone is not the dominant factor; rather, performance is governed by the interaction between the coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) and interlayer compatibility. ABF-L engineering materials demonstrate minimal warpage when used as substrate dielectrics. Among solder materials, Sn63Pb37 exhibits the lowest equivalent stress at 29.007 MPa under identical conditions but accumulates the highest plastic strain at 6.3659 × 10−2, making it susceptible to plastic deformation. This compromises fatigue life and reliability, increasing the long-term risk of substrate warpage.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: In recent years, electronic packaging has played increasingly critical roles in chip interconnection, physical support, and meeting growing market demands. Product development trends now prioritize miniaturization, lightweight designs, and multifunctionality, which drive the need for more precise fabrication of packaging substrates with higher density and thinner layer stacks1,2. System-in-Package (SiP) technology has emerged as an effective solution to these challenges by integrating diverse semiconductor processes and technologies. SiP enables standard packages to deliver enhanced functionality while satisfying demands for high-density integration3. As a result, multilayer Printed Circuit Boards (PCBs) have become superior to single or double-sided PCBs in accommodating complex electronic circuits. Typically, multilayer PCBs consist of solder mask layers, dielectric layers, and Redistribution Layer (RDL) copper traces. However, during high-temperature reflow soldering processes, warpage readily occurs due to coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) mismatches between alternating copper and dielectric layers. This deformation can cause severe failures, including short circuits and open bonding bridges, ultimately reducing device service life4.

A substantial number of researchers have dedicated their efforts to tackling these challenges. For instance, S. Huber and colleagues5 utilized Finite Element Modeling (FEM) in conjunction with shadow moiré techniques to conduct an in-depth analysis of molded packages. Shaikh et al.6 discovered that while lidded SiP modules can effectively mitigate warpage, they also introduce new concerns, particularly those related to thermal management. Chen et al.7 integrated the Cross-Castro-Macosko viscosity model with the Kamal curing kinetics model to investigate warpage under varying process parameters, demonstrating that accounting for interaction effects yields more precise results, with deviations from experimental data kept within 15%. Takahashi et al.8 performed FEM analyses on various encapsulant materials and structures, demonstrating that materials with lower glass transition temperatures and higher elastic moduli effectively mitigate warpage. Both dielectric and copper circuit layers exhibit orthotropic anisotropy9,10, with temperature and time identified as critical influencing factors. Additionally, polymer curing shrinkage during manufacturing plays a significant role in warpage formation. Oota et al.9 developed a curing shrinkage prediction model for Ball Grid Arrays (BGAs), confirming curing shrinkage as a major contributor to warpage. Hu et al.12 highlighted that simulations considering only thermal contraction introduce significant inaccuracies, while chemical curing shrinkage exerts a stronger influence on warpage in IC packages.

Traditional SiP research often simplifies polymer materials such as dielectrics and epoxy molding compounds (EMCs) as linear elastic, which reduces computational complexity but introduces notable discrepancies between simulation results and actual warpage behavior. Incorporating viscoelastic modeling captures long-term deformation and stress relaxation, significantly improving predictive accuracy. Wang et al.13 characterized substrate warpage using generalized Maxwell models, which outperform linear elastic models in simulating warpage-induced stresses. However, generalized Maxwell models alone cannot fully capture the complex viscoelastic responses of these materials. Lin and Hwang14 addressed this limitation by integrating temperature shift factors and conversion factors into generalized Maxwell models, accounting for time-, temperature-, and cure-dependent viscoelasticity in EMCs. In addition to viscoelastic effects, creep—a common mechanical behavior under operational conditions—can cause long-term deformation, structural instability, and material degradation15–18.

Despite these advances, several limitations remain. Wang et al.19 only analyzed variations in solder ball geometry during reflow, while Nguyen et al.20. combined experimental studies on BGA reliability with FEM simulations under thermal cycling conditions. Much of the existing research treats substrate warpage and reflow analysis independently, oversimplifying models by neglecting detailed copper trace geometries and assuming linear dielectric behavior. Critically, the combined effects of temperature-dependent viscoelasticity in dielectric layers and solder creep behavior have yet to be fully explored, leaving a significant gap in SiP packaging research. In addition, Lee et al.21 demonstrated that within the range of 0.35 mm to 0.55 mm, a 0.4 mm copper pillar bump represents the optimal choice, as it significantly enhances interconnection reliability during the reflow soldering process. Concurrently, Razzaq et al.22 employed finite element simulations to validate that a higher solidification temperature leads to increased residual stress, and the level of solidification temperature directly influences the failure location.

To address this gap, this study employs Finite Element Method (FEM) modeling to establish a SiP simulation incorporating detailed copper trace geometries. Multiphysics-coupled simulations are performed, integrating curing kinetics, viscoelastic behavior, and reflow soldering processes under various conditions. This comprehensive approach enables investigation into the evolution of temperature distributions, stress-strain relationships, and warpage deformation across all SiP components, while clarifying the interaction between substrate warpage and solder ball performance. Traditional finite element analysis blindly pursues simplified models, resulting in insufficient accuracy and large deviations from experiments; while pursuing high-precision complex models will lead to a large amount of computation and even insufficient computing power.The combined analysis of viscoelastic and other constitutive models using Trace mapping technology proposed in this paper can effectively improve accuracy while reducing the demand for computing power, thus providing practical guidance for engineering applications.

sec.title: SiP finite element model
sec.p: Figure 1 illustrates the schematic structure of the SiP package, while Fig. 2 presents the corresponding 3D simulation model. The SiP package analyzed in this study features a high-density substrate fabricated using the Semi-Additive Process (SAP), consisting of twelve redistribution layers (RDLs) stacked on a core substrate. The thickness of each layer is summarized in Table 1. Three silicon dies of varying sizes—5 × 6 mm, 11 × 5 mm, and 5 × 4.7 mm—each with a thickness of 680 μm, are mounted on the top surface of the substrate. Solder balls are attached to the bottom surface, each with a diameter of 100 μm and a standoff height of 200 μm. The Cu pads for the solder balls are modeled as homogeneous blocks with a thickness of 20 μm and side lengths of 36 μm. The entire PCB measures 38 mm × 38 mm with a total thickness of 16 mm. Additional detailed specifications are provided in the accompanying figures.

sec.title: Material properties for SiP package
sec.p: Warpage is typically induced by the total material strain23. However, existing research often focuses primarily on the linear elastic characteristics of materials, frequently neglecting the contribution of thermally-induced strain and curing-induced strain to warpage formation. This relationship can be represented by the following formula:
Formula (1): : total strain matrix;: elastic strain matrix༛༚heat-induced strain matrix༛༚Curing induced strain matrix.

It is assumed that the dielectric layer material in the substrate is linearly elastic, homogeneous, and isotropic. The fundamental stress-strain relationship is represented by the generalized Hook’s law:
Formula (3) : stress matrix; : stiffness matrix; : Total Strain Matrix.

For polymer materials in electronic packaging, volume shrinkage is typically neglected due to its minimal impact on overall results. This study primarily focuses on the viscoelastic behavior of these polymeric materials. The substrate used in this research was provided in collaboration with Accelink Meiwave Electronics (Suzhou) Co., Ltd. The unit cell model consists of alternating layers of elastic material (copper) and viscoelastic material (ABF). The dielectric material ABF exhibits viscoelastic behavior, combining the elastic characteristics of solids with the viscous flow properties of fluids. The mechanical response of polymers is generally time-dependent, a phenomenon known as stress relaxation, where stress gradually decreases over time under constant strain. Although stress relaxation can be described by the classic Maxwell model24, which consists of a Hookean spring and a Newtonian dashpot in series, this simple representation is insufficient for capturing the complex viscoelastic behavior of polymer materials. To overcome this limitation, the Generalized Maxwell model is adopted in Fig. 3, where multiple Maxwell elements are connected in parallel25,26. This model enables a more accurate representation of viscoelastic behavior and can be expressed in both time and frequency domains through the following equations:

caption.p: Generalized Maxwell model.

sec.p: Typically, the parameters in the equations above are obtained by fitting experimental data. However, practical challenges arise, as it is often difficult to experimentally measure creep or stress relaxation behavior over the broad time or frequency ranges required. To address this limitation, the Time-Temperature Superposition (TTS) principle is employed. This method enables the construction of a master curve by shifting data collected at various temperatures, effectively extending the observable time or frequency range. The relationship between the temperature shift factor () and temperature is commonly described by the Williams–Landel–Ferry (WLF) Eqs27,28:

where T is the reference temperature, Tg (glass transition temperature) is taken, and c1 and c2 are the material constants, where c1 and c2 are the material constants that depend on the specific material, and is the offset factor of the ratio of the relaxation time between the reference temperature and the specific temperature T.

The fundamental cause of warpage differences lies in the dominant role of the viscoelastic model in governing deformation under high-temperature loading. When polymer materials are heated to elevated temperatures and maintained for a certain duration, internal residual stresses gradually dissipate through viscous flow, meaning the material’s relaxation modulus decreases over time, thereby reducing warpage caused by internal stress inhomogeneity. For materials with fast relaxation29, the stress rapidly attenuates to an equilibrium value, leading to near-complete stress release and essentially “setting” the warpage shortly after molding. In contrast, for materials with slow relaxation30, the opposite occurs—the extent of warpage reduction is significantly influenced by the duration of subsequent curing stages. Of particular relevance to the current discussion is the work by Lin et al.31, who utilized Moldex3D software and a constitutive model for the Epoxy Molding Compound (EMC) to conduct a detailed analysis of warpage and residual stress. Their study specifically investigated the effects induced by temperature and curing during the IC encapsulation molding and Post-Mold Cure (PMC) processes. A key finding was that the duration of the PMC and the specific PMC temperature had a relatively minor influence on the observed warpage and residual stress. This outcome strongly suggests that for the material studied, which likely exhibits fast relaxation, the internal stress and resulting warpage rapidly decayed and reached a stable equilibrium value early in the process, thereby diminishing the significance of subsequent variations in PMC parameters.

Figure 4 illustrates typical volume changes during the thermosetting cure cycle, alongside molecular structure snapshots at various reaction conversion stages: (a) 0%, (b) 20%, (c) 40%, (d) 50%, (e) 60%, and (f) 70%. Chemically bonded molecular segments are shown in distinct colors. The severity of warpage correlates with the Degree of Cure (DOC). This study focuses on stages b–c–d–e in Fig. 4, demonstrating the molecular evolution of thermosets during curing and the corresponding volume changes. During heating from ambient temperature to near-curing temperature (a–b), polymer thermal expansion occurs. In the isothermal curing stage (b–c), van der Waals bonds are progressively replaced by covalent bonds, forming crosslinked networks and reducing intermolecular distances. Subsequent cooling (c–e) leads to polymer thermal contraction. The slope change in this stage reflects distinct behavior before and after the glass transition temperature (T < sub> g</sub> ). Final volumetric shrinkage (e–a stage) results from both chemical shrinkage and resin-specific thermal expansion effects. Therefore, post-cure cooling shrinkage must be accurately modeled in substrate encapsulation simulations. While polymers exhibit accelerated thermal expansion above T < sub> g</sub>, practical softening (approaching fluid-like zero-stress states) requires explicit simulation considerations32–35. Figure 5 presents molecular snapshots of epoxy resin from the initial reaction (0%) to high conversion (70%)36. Microscopically, isolated molecular fragments (color-coded) gradually form covalent bonds, evolving into a continuous 3D network (blue regions). During crosslinking (e–f stage), covalent bonding reduces molecular spacing beyond the vitrification point, where volumetric shrinkage halts and internal stresses begin to accumulate. This sequence provides a detailed understanding of the micro-mechanism behind cure-induced shrinkage stress in dielectric layers, which ultimately drives substrate warpage. Additional parameters are provided in Table 2, with material properties obtained through collaborative testing.

sec.p: The interaction between solder joints and warpage during the packaging process is mutually dependent. In the SiP package examined, Sn63Pb37 solder is used for the solder joints. The strain behavior of these joints is governed by both creep and plasticity, with their mechanical response under thermal loading exhibiting Viscoplastic characteristics. Anand37 and Brown38 proposed constitutive models to describe anisotropic and Viscoplastic deformation, with the Anand model uniquely integrating both time-independent plasticity and time-dependent Viscoplastic phenomena. In this model, the evolution of plastic strain is influenced by the loading rate, while Viscoplasticity reflects the combined effects of creep and plastic deformation. The Anand model utilizes internal state variables to capture isotropic hardening mechanisms, including subgrain and grain size effects, dislocation density, and solid solution strengthening. Research indicates that the material’s behavior is highly sensitive to strain rate, temperature, and the combined effects of strain hardening and softening. Therefore, this study adopts the Anand Viscoplastic constitutive model, embedded within ANSYS software, to accurately characterize the complex mechanical behavior of solder joints. This model offers several distinct advantages39:

sec.p: The Redistribution Layer (RDL) in the package substrate consists of fine copper (Cu) traces embedded within the dielectric ABF material. Due to the intricate complexity of these Cu trace patterns, direct and detailed geometric modeling becomes impractical. As a result, some researchers have adopted equivalent material modeling approaches, homogenizing the properties of the Cu traces and dielectric layers. While this simplifies the modeling process, it often leads to significant discrepancies between simulation results and experimental measurements. Kim et al.27 introduced a viscoelastic modeling approach using an orthotropic viscoelastic shell method to model multi-layer PCBs. In their approach, orthotropic copper circuit layers were discretized into uniformly sized elements. Representative Cu pattern shapes were selected, and effective thermomechanical properties for each representative pattern were calculated and assigned to the corresponding regions in the model. The complete PCB structure, including the FR-4 core and PSR (Photo-Solder Resist) layers, was then modeled, and warpage simulations were performed under reflow temperature conditions. Although this method improved simulation accuracy to some extent, notable discrepancies with experimental results still persisted.

Figure 6 illustrates the Cu line mapping. Traditional methods often simplify copper traces using homogenization techniques, which significantly reduces accuracy. In contrast, this study adopts the Trace Mapping technique to model the Cu trace layers. This method offers a simpler and more practical approach, improving modeling efficiency while maintaining sufficient accuracy.

caption.p: Cu line mapping: (a) real Cu circuit diagram; (b) Mapping top view; (c) Side view.

sec.p: Using ANSYS software, the stack-up design files were processed and the model was divided into layers. This study focuses on a high-density multilayer substrate with a 5 + 2+5 configuration, which was segmented into 12 layers corresponding to the stack-up described in Table 1, as shown in Fig. 6c. A reference coordinate system was established to ensure precision during the copper trace mapping process, preventing deviations. The mapping result is displayed in Fig. 6b. It is important to ensure that the mapping aligns correctly with the model and the stack-up design; otherwise, the results may be compromised or erroneous.

Figure 7 presents the mesh model along with its partitioning scheme. A multi-region meshing strategy was adopted in this study. Given the complexity of the model and the large number of components, coarser mesh elements were assigned to non-critical regions that are not central to the primary analysis. In contrast, mesh refinement was applied to areas subject to higher stress gradients or localized deformation. For example, since stress concentrations primarily occur at the corners of the solder joints, these regions, particularly the corner solder balls, were meshed with a higher density, as shown in Fig. 7c. This approach of applying differential mesh refinement based on expected mechanical behavior and regional importance was consistently implemented throughout the model.

caption.p: Mesh model division diagram: (a) main view; (b) Side view; (c) Partial enlargement of the solder ball mesh.

sec.p: Figure 8 is a mesh convergence analysis diagram. In finite element analysis, the impact of mesh convergence on results is critical, with the convergence criterion generally defined as a residual threshold of less than 5%. Solutions are deemed converged once the error falls below this threshold. Based on this foundation, a mesh convergence study was performed. The results showed that the 1.05-mm mesh size yielded the highest error, while the 0.1-mm mesh size reached convergence. However, excessively refined meshes significantly increase computing time. Balancing computational efficiency while maintaining sufficient accuracy is essential.

caption.p: Mesh convergence analysis diagram.

sec.p: As shown in Fig. 8; Table 4, the warpage is 21.1 μm with a mesh size of 0.35 mm and 20.9 μm with a mesh size of 0.1 mm, representing a difference of only 0.95%, which is significantly lower than the 5% defined by the convergence criterion. However, the computation time for the 0.1 mm mesh size is as high as 98,280 s, compared to 47,000 s for the 0.35 mm mesh size—more than double the duration. In contrast, with a mesh size of 0.7 mm, the computation time is only 2,160 s, but the resulting warpage value is 22.8 μm, differing by 8.05% from the reference result and exceeding the 5% threshold set by the convergence criterion. Therefore, to ensure both efficiency and reliability, subsequent simulations adopted a 0.35-mm mesh size for discretization.

caption.p: Quantitative analysis of mesh convergence.

sec.p: For the reflow warpage simulation, an ambient temperature of 25 °C was assumed. The thermal loading profile begins at room temperature (25 °C), rises to a peak of 240 °C, and then cools back to the starting temperature. This specific reflow temperature profile is representative of processes used for high-end, miniaturized electronic products, as illustrated in the reflow process curve shown in Fig. 9.

caption.p: Reflow soldering process curve.

sec.p: To replicate real-world boundary conditions during reflow soldering, a three-point constraint method was applied to the PCB base27:
Point A: Fully constrained in all directions (x = y = z = 0).
Point B: Constrained in the x-direction (x = 0; y and z free).
Point C: Constrained in the y-direction (y = 0; x and z free).
A schematic representation of these constraints is provided in Fig. 10.

caption.p: Displacement constraint at three points.

sec.p: While the simulation results offer valuable insights for practical manufacturing, simplifications in the models and material properties were necessary due to experimental limitations and computational constraints. The key assumptions made in this study are as follows:
All materials, including Cu trace layers, were assumed homogeneous within each thermal loading step.
The ABF dielectric material was modeled with nonlinear, temperature-dependent properties.
The PCB and core layer materials were treated as orthotropic, whereas all other materials were assumed linear elastic and isotropic.
All material interfaces were considered perfectly bonded, with no delamination or interfacial slip.

All components were assumed to be in a stress-free state at the initial temperature of 25 °C, except for polymer composites (such as organic PCB substrates and dielectric layers), where curing-induced residual stresses were accounted for using viscoelastic models. This initial temperature also serves as the starting point for the reflow profile.
Accumulated principal stresses within components during the reflow process were neglected.
The solder bumps (balls) and their underlying Cu pads were simplified and modeled as an equivalent monolithic block.

Based on the simulation approach described above, this study conducted analyses on existing products with similar architectures. Figure 11 presents a comparison between simulation results and experimental measurements. The experimental data, obtained using the Shadow Moiré technique, demonstrated a simulation error within 20%, which is considered acceptable for the intended application. Therefore, the same simulation methodology is applied in this study to predict warpage behavior in higher-end SiP packaging substrates and assemblies.

caption.p: Verification of simulation results.

sec.title: Analysis of warpage stress results for SiP package during reflow soldering process
sec.p: Figure 12 compares the simulated warpage of the substrate during the reflow soldering process with and without considering the initial warpage. The results show that when the initial warpage is considered, the maximum warpage at the end of reflow reaches 29.3 μm, which is well below the IPC-6012 warpage standard (< 0.75%). Compared to the initial warpage of 25.6 μm, the warpage increased by 3.7 μm after reflow. As shown in Fig. 12a, the residual warpage after reflow is very similar to the initial warpage in both magnitude and profile.

caption.p: Substrate simulation warpage results during reflow soldering: (a) warpage profile; (b) Plot of the maximum warpage curve at reflow temperature.

sec.p: Both warpage-free and initial-warpage cases display a “smiling face” profile (concave center, elevated edges) at the peak reflow temperature. In contrast, the initial heating and post-cooling stages exhibit a “frowning face” profile (convex center, depressed edges), as thermal expansion governs warpage behavior at high temperatures, causing downward center deflection during heating. As temperature increases beyond Tg, dielectric materials soften into viscoelastic states, transitioning toward near-zero stress levels, which limits further warpage growth — consistent with Do-Hyoung Kim’s SSD simulation trends27.

At the peak temperature of 240 °C, warpage reaches 94.9 μm for the warpage-free condition and 36.7 μm for the initial warpage case, with the former exceeding the latter by 58.2 μm. Post-cooling, while thermal expansion effects subside, Fig. 12b shows a slight warpage rebound at room temperature, attributed to ongoing crosslinking-induced residual stress accumulation. Experimental validation confirms that residual warpage is highly sensitive to the initial warpage condition. Residual warpage induced during earlier process stages (e.g., pre-curing) can lead to serious assembly defects, such as solder bridging, open joints, and cracking. Therefore, ignoring initial warpage underestimates cumulative warpage in multi-stage manufacturing and leads to overly optimistic simulation predictions. As shown in Figs. 12b and 13b, the warpage values differ by 25.8 μm and 93 μm, respectively, between the models with and without initial warpage. This significant discrepancy occurs because the model incorporating initial warpage accounts for the viscoelastic properties of the polymer materials, which exhibit a delayed warpage growth mechanism. Since key materials in the package assembly, such as the ABF dielectric layer and the PCB substrate, inherently possess this characteristic, failure to account for these polymer properties will inevitably lead to increased deviation in the simulation results.This result is consistent with the discussion in the previous chapter on viscoelasticity30.

caption.p: The overall simulation warpage results of the package during the reflow soldering process: (a) warpage profile; (b) Plot of the maximum warpage curve at reflow temperature.

sec.p: Figure 13 shows the full-assembly warpage simulation during reflow soldering. In addition to the substrate, reflow establishes permanent mechanical and electrical interconnections between solder balls and the full assembly. Due to computational constraints, certain simplifications were applied—solder bumps were modeled as homogeneous bulk structures, and pads as solid copper plates. Nevertheless, Fig. 13a reveals warpage contours consistent with Fig. 12a: a “frowning face” profile dominates at peak reflow, while “smiling face” contours appear during heating and cooling.

Importantly, adding components and solder joints significantly increases warpage magnitude and alters deformation modes. As shown in Fig. 13b, under initial warpage conditions, polymer shrinkage decreases while thermal expansion dominates, resulting in a transient warpage peak of 108.77 μm during mid-reflow—still within acceptable limits. After cooling, warpage partially recovers but rebounds to 93.56 μm at ambient temperature, exceeding the initial 81.58 μm by 12.02 μm. This delayed warpage growth results from the combined effects of residual soldering stresses and ongoing polymer curing shrinkage, producing progressive warpage intensification during cooling.

sec.title: Experimental verification
sec.p: Figure 14 presents a comparison between experimental and simulation results for the SiP substrate: (a) SiP substrate experimental results; (b) SiP substrate simulation results; (c) SiP substrate product. Based on the substrate warpage simulation study mentioned above (referring to Fig. 12), experimental validation was conducted using the Shadow Moiré technique. The results indicate that the actual product warpage was 31.5 μm, while the simulated warpage was 29.3737 μm. The overall difference between the results considering the initial warpage and the actual product is only 6.75%. Specifically, the difference in the maximum warpage value is 6.38%, and the difference in the minimum warpage value is 16.35%. These errors are significantly lower than the internationally recognized 20% threshold. Compared with the 10–20% simulation errors reported by Lee et al.23 and Chen et al.7 in their studies on SiP packaging, the method proposed in this study demonstrates higher accuracy, fully validating the reliability of the research approach. However, it is important to note that the complete SiP component product has not yet been realized, preventing experimental validation at this stage. Furthermore, this study employs assumptions such as perfect interfacial contact, and its conclusions regarding model accuracy are specific to the constructed framework. Therefore, future work should involve testing the methodology on a wider variety of model architectures and incorporating deep learning techniques, such as PI-LSTM, to assist the research.

caption.p: presents a comparison between experimental and simulation results for the SiP substrate.

sec.title: Sensitivity analysis
sec.p: A comparison of Fig. 14b, d reveals that the model using the Trace Mapping technique yields more accurate results than the model using the homogenized equivalent method. The error between the Trace Mapping technique and the experimental results is only 6.35%, whereas the error for the homogenized equivalent method is 16.56%—a difference of 10.21% points. This discrepancy arises because the homogenized method only equivalates the copper trace material properties. However, the warpage outcome depends not only on material properties but also significantly on the internal copper trace structure. As can be seen in Fig. 6a Real Cu circuit diagram, the copper traces act like a “spider-web” or reinforcement bars in concrete, providing a strengthening effect that effectively restrains deformation caused by thermal expansion. Thus, the homogenized method, which amplifies material properties while neglecting the structural role, is less accurate. Furthermore, the warpage shapes in Fig. 14a, d differ. The warpage shape from the homogenized equivalent model is a very standard “crying face” pattern, highest in the center and lowest at the edges. However, observation of the experimental result in Fig. 14a indicates that the actual warpage manifests more as a “wavy” pattern. This is because the irregular distribution of internal copper traces creates localized variations in their constraining effect—a detail that the homogenized equivalent model cannot capture. This study also has limitations, as factors such as the assumption of “perfect interfacial contact” were not deeply investigated.

sec.title: Stress analysis
sec.p: Figure 15 shows the stress-induced warpage contours of the fully assembled package during the reflow soldering process. At the peak reflow temperature of 240 °C, the assembly was constrained using the three-point method previously described (see Fig. 12). Stress concentrations are primarily located beneath the chip component, particularly at the interface between the silicon die and the redistribution layer (RDL). Simulation results reveal that at 240 °C, the maximum warpage-induced stress reaches 269.6 MPa at the die-to-substrate interface, driven by the severe material property mismatch between silicon and the substrate. However, this stress level remains well within design limits, as silicon’s tensile strength is 1100 MPa41.

caption.p: Stress warpage profile of the overall package of the reflow soldering process: (a) top view; (b) Side view (interlaminar stress layer).

sec.p: Beyond the primary stress concentration at the die-substrate junction, a highly non-uniform stress distribution emerges across the assembly. This non-uniformity is attributed to the intricate spider-web-like configuration of the copper RDL traces, which introduces heterogeneous residual stresses during cooling. As substrate materials contract more rapidly than copper during the cooling phase, these differential contractions create the observed stress patterns, improving the simulation’s alignment with real-world physical behavior.

Figure 16 presents the equivalent stress distribution within the solder balls at the final reflow temperature. The Sn63Pb37 solder alloy exhibits both compressive and tensile stresses due to package warpage, with the highest stresses (~ 30.125 MPa) occurring at the peripheral corners—areas subjected to the greatest warpage-induced deformation. The most critical stress regions are located at the top surfaces of the solder balls, where they interface with the substrate RDL. These regions are prone to crack initiation and interconnect failure, consistent with widely reported failure mechanisms in the literature.

caption.p: Contour of solder ball von mises stress distribution at final reflow temperature.

sec.title: Influence and analysis of substrate material properties during reflow soldering
sec.p: Based on the reflow soldering warpage analysis, this study investigates two key locations using three commonly employed process materials, with the following findings:

Table 5 shows that for the three core board materials tested under identical thermal expansion conditions, warpage increases with increasing elastic modulus. MCL-G, with the lowest elastic modulus, exhibits a warpage of 93.73 μm, while MCL-H, with the highest modulus, reaches 108.23 μm—an increase of 14.5 μm compared to MCL-G. This observation contrasts with conventional expectations where higher stiffness (elastic modulus) is typically associated with reduced warpage.

caption.p: Effect of core board material on package warpage.

sec.p: In reality, warpage results from the interaction between thermal stress and material stiffness. As temperature rises, the material exhibits significant anisotropy, with its coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) in the Z-direction far exceeding that in the X and Y directions. Calculations reveal that expansion in the Y-direction is approximately 15 times higher than in the other two directions. Consequently, residual stresses are primarily released along the Z-axis during heating. However, a higher modulus increases stiffness, making it harder for residual stress to relax, leading to greater warpage as a compensatory release mechanism. Thus, a higher elastic modulus may, counterintuitively, result in greater warpage. Moreover, selecting a core material with an appropriate modulus is essential to ensure compatibility with adjacent layers, such as the dielectric and copper layers, to avoid stiffness mismatch. Therefore, the highest modulus is not always the optimal choice for packaging substrates; matching surrounding material properties is critical.

Table 6 shows the effect of three dielectric layer materials on warpage. Based on this analysis, MCL-G was selected as the core board for further study. Three commonly used dielectric materials (ABF types) were then evaluated using material data provided by a partner company. The results show that ABF-Z exhibits the lowest warpage (41.73 μm), while ABF-Y has the highest (93.73 μm), with ABF-L falling in between. ABF-Z’s superior warpage performance is due to its higher Tg, greater brittleness, and moderate modulus, which help reduce residual stress. However, its higher CTE compared to ABF-L places its warpage performance between the other two. ABF-L, with the lowest CTE in the core temperature range (150 °C to 240 °C), experiences the least thermal expansion and contraction, reducing thermal mismatch and warpage.

caption.p: Effect of dielectric layer material on package warpage.

sec.p: Additionally, experimental measurements indicate that ABF-Z has significantly lower flexural endurance (bend count) than ABF-L. Therefore, material selection for packaging substrates must consider multiple factors based on product requirements. In this study, ABF-L is chosen as the dielectric layer material for the substrate. Warpage analysis incorporating solder ball effects will be addressed in the following section.

sec.title: Analysis of solder balls under reflow soldering
sec.p: Figure 17 shows the failure crack morphology of solder balls observed under a scanning electron microscope (SEM). Solder balls are critical components in reflow soldering, requiring careful control of microstructure (e.g., intermetallic compound (IMC) layer formation), geometric integrity, and stress distribution. Their integrity has a significant impact on substrate warpage and overall package reliability; fracture or misalignment of solder balls can substantially increase warpage and jeopardize the mechanical and electrical performance of the package. Therefore, detailed analysis of solder ball materials and their structural behavior is essential.

caption.p: Scanning electron microscope image of the failure mode of the solder joint during temperature cycling shows that cracks appear at the interface of the SN63PB37 solder ball module41.

sec.p: Due to environmental restrictions on traditional lead-based solder42, lead-free alternatives have become increasingly important. Based on previously optimized process parameters, this study investigated two anticipated lead-free alloy solders, SAC387 and SAC405, as well as the conventional Sn63Pb37 solder. The Anand Viscoplastic constitutive model is applied to capture the creep behavior of solder balls during the reflow process.

Figure 18 presents the simulation results for solder balls during reflow. As the reflow temperature reaches 240 °C, the polymer materials in the substrate achieve sufficient temperature for crosslinking and bonding, while solder balls enter a quasi-fluid state, resulting in a sharp decrease in stress. At the maximum reflow temperature, the stresses of Sn63Pb37, the expected lead-free solder alloys SAC387 and SAC405 are 7.787 MPa, 11.724 MPa, and 19.028 MPa, respectively. As cooling progresses, the stress levels of all solders remain relatively low during this stage, first decreasing and then gradually increasing. During cooling, polymer shrinkage from continued crosslinking and curing, combined with CTE mismatches among the materials, causes differential contraction rates and the accumulation of residual stress. Solder balls located at package corners experience the highest stresses, reaching maximum values at room temperature. Under identical boundary conditions, post-reflow equivalent stress is lowest for Sn63Pb37 at 29.007 MPa, while SAC405 exhibits the highest at 46.998 MPa. However, Sn63Pb37 also shows the highest plastic strain (6.3659 × 10−2). Lead-based solders have lower yield strength, making them more prone to plastic deformation, which facilitates stress relief during reflow but results in higher irreversible plastic strain. This increased plastic strain may lead to harmful failure modes, such as solder ball neck fracture, pad delamination, and significantly reduced fatigue life. In contrast, the lead-free solder alloy SAC405 is expected to exhibit the lowest plastic strain and better thermal expansion coefficient compatibility with the substrate, thereby improving overall structural stability. To further verify these findings, temperature cycling tests (− 4 °C to 120 °C) were conducted on Sn63Pb37, the anticipated lead-free solder alloys SAC387 and SAC405. After eight cycles, the measured plastic strain (Fig. 19) supports the conclusions of Depiver et al.43, confirming that lower plastic strain is associated with longer solder joint service life. In summary, the anticipated lead-free solder alloy SAC405 is a promising candidate material for substrate assembly, offering potential improvements in warpage control and extended service life, while meeting lead-free requirements.

caption.p: Simulation results under solder ball reflow soldering: (a) Equivalent stress result diagram; (b) Diagram of plastic strain results.
Plastic strain diagram of solder balls under temperature cycling.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In this study, the reflow soldering process for advanced SiP package components was simulated, incorporating trace mapping of actual copper layouts and considering material viscoelasticity and creep behavior. The effects of dielectric layers, core substrate materials, and solder ball parameters on warpage and stress were systematically investigated. The key conclusions are as follows:

Simulation results considering initial warpage and viscoelastic creep effects show that, compared with traditional models, its accuracy and reliability are significantly improved, with the error between substrate experiments and simulations being only 6.35%.

The elastic modulus of core board materials does not directly correlate with reduced warpage. Effective warpage control depends on the thermomechanical compatibility between core substrates and surrounding layers. The engineered dielectric material ABF-L was identified as the optimal choice, achieving the lowest warpage of 41.73 μm.

Sn63Pb37 solder shows the lowest von Mises stress (29.007 MPa) but exhibits the highest plastic strain (6.37 × 10−2), resulting in the shortest fatigue life, increased risk of solder joint failure, and higher long-term substrate warpage. In contrast, the anticipated lead-free solder alloys SAC405 solder demonstrates the lowest plastic strain and offers improved long-term reliability, making it the recommended material for robust assembly.

The findings of this research offer valuable guidance for the design, material selection, and development of advanced System-in-Package (SiP) solutions. Regarding the current study, although it has significantly improved accuracy and reduced computational load, it still relies on traditional computational methods, resulting in high computational complexity. In future research, we aim to incorporate machine learning to assist in calculations—for example, using PI-LSTM to predict the stress of solder balls under thermal cycling—to enhance computational efficiency while maintaining accuracy.
